problem:
Meridian Bank wants more new retail customers to complete digital onboarding, but only a small share of started applications reach an active account. Customers abandon the journey at document upload and at identity verification, and many who do finish are later held for manual review because documents are unclear or data does not match. The compliance team is worried that simplifying the journey will weaken controls, while the product team is worried that every extra step loses customers.

The redesign must map where customers drop out, which documents are genuinely needed for each customer type, how validation and screening work, and what happens when something fails. It must also measure conversion properly, so the bank can tell whether a change helped customers or only moved the failure to a later step.
solution:
Start with evidence, not opinions. Measure the funnel stage by stage: started, identity details entered, document uploaded, identity verified, screening complete, account opened and first transaction. Break dropout down by device, document type, customer segment and failure reason, so the team fixes the actual causes instead of the loudest complaint.

Collect documents by customer type and risk, not by a single long list for everyone. Ask for each document once, explain why it is needed and what a good capture looks like, and validate quality at capture so a blurred image is retaken immediately rather than failing hours later in manual review. Run identity verification, document validation and sanctions and adverse-media screening in a clear order, and show the customer a plain-language status at each stage.

Design exception handling as part of the journey, not as an afterthought. A failed check should tell the customer exactly what to do next, offer a supported alternative such as a different document or an assisted channel, and preserve the application so the customer does not start again. Route genuinely risky or unclear cases to trained reviewers with the full evidence pack, and set service levels for review so applications do not stall silently. Measure conversion, time to account opening, manual review rate and rework rate after every change, and only keep changes that improve completion without increasing bad outcomes.

decision.question: Meridian Bank is redesigning digital KYC onboarding. Dropout is highest at document upload and identity verification, and many completed applications stall in manual review. What is the best redesign approach?

options.label: A
options.detail: Add more document requirements so manual review has more evidence.

options.label: B
options.detail: Map dropout and failure points, collect only the documents needed for each customer type, validate and screen in stages with clear guidance and exception handling, and measure conversion end to end.

options.label: C
options.detail: Keep the journey unchanged and increase marketing spend to bring in more starters.

options.label: D
options.detail: Remove document upload and identity checks to maximise completion.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because it reduces friction where it is caused by poor guidance or unnecessary requirements, while keeping validation and screening controls intact and measuring the real outcome. Option D removes controls and creates compliance risk. Option A increases friction and manual review load. Option C spends more to feed the same broken journey.

steps.title: Starts onboarding in the app and enters personal details
Determines the documents and checks required for this customer type and risk level
Captures identity document with on-screen quality guidance
Validates the document and matches the customer identity
Runs sanctions, adverse-media and fraud screening
Decides the outcome: approve, request a correction, or route to manual review
Reviews referred applications with the full evidence pack
Opens the account, confirms the outcome to the customer and records the audit trail

happy: The customer enters details once, captures a clear document with live guidance, passes identity verification and screening, and the account opens in the same session. The customer receives a clear confirmation and can transact immediately, and the full evidence pack is stored for audit.

negative.title: Poor document capture
negative.detail: The image is blurred or cropped, so validation fails. Detect quality at capture, explain the problem in plain language, and let the customer retake the image immediately without restarting the application.

negative.title: Data mismatch
negative.detail: The name or date of birth on the document does not match the entered details. Show exactly which field differs, let the customer correct it or choose a matching document, and route unresolved mismatches to manual review with both values visible.

negative.title: Screening hit
negative.detail: Screening returns a possible match that needs judgement. Hold the application in a defined review state, give the reviewer the screening evidence and the customer record, and do not auto-reject on a possible match alone.

negative.title: Application abandoned
negative.detail: The customer leaves part-way through and returns later. Preserve the application and its documents securely, let the customer resume where they stopped, and send a single helpful reminder rather than repeated prompts.

technical: Keep one onboarding case record with a stable application ID, the customer type, the required document set, each check result and its timestamp, and the final decision with its reason. Validate document quality, format and expiry at capture, and store documents securely with retention rules. Use structured customer data with clear field definitions, and record the source of every data value so a mismatch can be traced. Make screening calls idempotent and record the screening reference and result version. Separate the decision outcome from the channel display so a screen error cannot be mistaken for a rejection. Log every access to customer documents for audit, and mask sensitive data in logs and support screens.

accounting: Onboarding has no customer funds movement, so the operational impact is in worklists, service levels and audit. Referred applications sit on a reviewer worklist with an owner, an age and a target review time, and aged items escalate. No account may be opened until the required checks for that customer type are recorded as passed or formally overridden with approval. Rejected applications keep their evidence and reason for the required retention period. Report conversion, manual review rate, average time to open and rework rate weekly, and treat a rise in manual review as a signal to fix guidance or validation, not as a reason to loosen checks.

questions.question: What is the first step in redesigning a KYC journey?
options: Measure the funnel stage by stage and find where and why customers drop out or fail.
questions.explanation: Evidence about dropout and failure reasons shows which steps actually cause the problem.

questions.question: Why validate document quality at capture?
options: So a poor image is retaken immediately instead of failing hours later in manual review.
questions.explanation: Early quality checks prevent avoidable manual review and long waits for the customer.

questions.question: How should a possible screening match be handled?
options: Ignore it and open the account.
Route it to manual review with the full screening evidence for a judged decision.
questions.explanation: A possible match needs human judgement with the evidence visible. Auto-rejection on a possible match alone is wrong.

questions.question: Which measure shows whether a redesign really worked?
options: Number of screens in the journey.
End-to-end conversion to an active account, with manual review rate and time to open.
questions.explanation: Starts alone can rise while completion falls. Conversion, review rate and time to open together show the real outcome.
